claims.text: Protective-oxide formation in high-entropy alloys is governed by preferential outward diffusion of chromium.
A sufficiently high chromium concentration causes formation of a continuous Cr2O3 layer.
A Cr2O3 barrier suppresses oxidation of less-protective elements such as Mn and prevents formation of non-protective oxides.
The proposed initial CrMnFeCoNi alloy has a homogeneous distribution of alloying elements.
The controlled intervention is to compare increased- and reduced-chromium variants while otherwise holding alloy composition constant.
At approximately 950°C or above, diffusion is active and oxidation kinetics are significant.
The relevant structural mediator is a compact, adherent Cr2O3 surface layer.
A continuous Cr2O3 scale impedes oxygen ingress.
Lower chromium levels permit Mn oxidation and formation of non-protective Mn3O4.
Increasing chromium will produce a more continuous protective Cr2O3 scale than reducing chromium.
Chromium-enhanced alloys will exhibit lower oxidation weight gain than chromium-reduced alloys.
Chromium-enhanced alloys will retain mechanical integrity better than chromium-reduced alloys.
The standard CrMnFeCoNi alloy tends to form a non-protective Mn3O4-containing scale during high-temperature oxidation.
The hypothesis applies at approximately 950°C and above where diffusion-controlled oxidation is dominant.
The hypothesis may not apply at lower temperatures or where other degradation mechanisms dominate.
Cr2O3 has a compact structure and provides superior oxidation resistance as an oxide barrier.
In the cited CrMnFeCoNi study, Cr2O3 was not detected and its absence was inferred to permit outward Mn diffusion and Mn3O4 formation at 950°C.
Non-protective oxide formation and Mn depletion may degrade the high-temperature mechanical performance of CrMnFeCoNi.
The quantitative effects of chromium concentration on diffusion kinetics and scale thickness, and the modifying effects of other alloying elements, remain unresolved.
Failure of increased chromium to produce a continuous Cr2O3 scale or significantly lower weight gain than reduced chromium would falsify the hypothesis.
